q: How do you sell a tool that can make anything?
lines: A tool that can make anything gives a visitor nothing to ask for.
So the front page stops describing the machine.
It shows a handful of tools already made, each one ready to run or to change.
quote: What are you really good at?
close: We find the few things a product does that make someone say: I need that.
alt: The front page, with tools already made

q: How do you get someone to write the first word?
lines: An empty box asks for the hardest thing first.
Nobody was ready to describe a tool from nothing.
So the first act became changing a tool somebody else had made.
quote: We believe that new users will not be prepared to create from a blank prompt at first
close: We find the smallest first move a newcomer will really make, and start the product there.
alt: The seventh bet: remixing is the new creating

q: How do you teach a product nobody has seen before?
lines: The old product only worked with someone sitting beside you.
So that someone went into the product.
You ask while you build, and the lesson is the work.
quote: If you weren’t here to walk me through it, I would have dropped off already.
close: We make the explanation part of the product, so nobody has to read before they start.
alt: A question being answered inside the build

q: How do you get someone to give up a habit that works?
lines: Nobody was waiting for this. They had a search bar and a dozen free tools.
So the product is not sold as something new. It is the same job, done in one place.
And we wrote down how we would know: do people who come for one tool stay for a second?
quote: a new way of completing an existing behavior to users, not a new behavior
close: We design against what people already do, not against an empty space.
alt: The first bet: a behavior change

q: How do you build for the expert without shutting out the beginner?
lines: The team wanted power users. Most visitors were not.
We did not thin the product down.
We gave it stairs: run a tool, change one, write one, chain them.
quote: Favor enabling power users over simplifying for casual users.
close: We keep the depth, and build the way up to it.
alt: The fourth bet: completeness over simplicity

q: What do you do when the machine gets it wrong?
lines: A failed run was a red box and nowhere to go.
Each one spent a little of the trust the product needed.
So every failure was given words, and a next move.
quote: feels like a dead end
from: the research, on a failed run
close: We design the bad moments first, because that is where people decide whether to come back.
alt: A run in progress, step by step

q: How do you know a design is right before anyone has used it?
lines: You don't. So we wrote down what we believed.
Eight bets about how people would behave, each with what would prove it wrong.
Every screen is one of those bets, built so the team can watch it win or lose.
quote: it is valuable to see if this hypothesis holds true
close: We hand over the reasoning with the screens, so the testing goes on after we leave.
alt: A bet, and how to test it

q: How do you let a machine do the work and leave the person in charge?
lines: People wanted it done for them. They were also afraid to touch what it wrote.
So the machine proposes, and the person decides.
One step, Review: take it, change it, or ask why.
quote: I did not modify the new prompt because I was scared to break anything.
close: We decide, move by move, who is holding the pen.
alt: The fifth bet: defer to the human

q: How do you make a wait feel like work being done?
lines: Building a tool takes minutes, and the screen said almost nothing.
People wondered whether to leave.
So the build shows who is on it: one plans, one writes, one checks.
quote: Things are happening. But how long should I wait for?
from: the team, walking the old flow
close: We design the minutes when nothing is asked of you.
alt: The old flow for building a tool

q: How do you say what you are in a few words?
lines: A new kind of product has no category to borrow.
Every candidate drew the box a little wrong: too small, too vague, too much about AI.
Dozens later, one line could hold it.
quote: these arent AI tools though. They are tools made with AI.
from: a note on the second round
close: We write the headline as a design problem, until the product fits inside it.
alt: Headline candidates

q: How do you talk to people who don't have your words?
lines: The product spoke in functions and integrations.
The people it was for did not.
So a function became a tool, and the first box asks you to describe one.
quote: Create a function that... I don’t know what a function is.
from: the team, walking the old flow
close: We take the team's vocabulary out and put the user's in.
alt: The first box: Describe your tool

q: How do you turn someone looking around into someone making things?
lines: It does not happen in one visit.
First they ask what this does. Then when it could help them. Then which of their problems it can keep solving.
Each part of the product was built for one of those questions.
quote: What of my problems can be consistently solved by this system
close: We map the change of mind first, then give each stage its place in the product.
alt: The journey model

q: How do you serve the person who knows what they want, and the one who doesn't?
lines: One came to build. One came to look.
Every page could only lead with one of them.
We chose the builder, and gave the looker a way to become one.
quote: Favor people who have a goal to complete, and secondarily support people who are curious or idly browsing
close: We choose who comes first, and then hold to it on every page.
alt: The third bet: intent over curiosity

q: How do you fix the onboarding when the onboarding isn't the problem?
lines: We were asked to clean up the onboarding.
The trouble sat earlier: nothing stood between hearing about the product and an empty box.
So we did not add a tour. We built what was missing in between.
quote: Today journey largely skips over middle, goes from ‘learn capabilities’ to ‘create’
close: We answer the brief by finding the problem underneath it.
alt: The scope of work, page by page

q: How do you make room for an idea that isn't finished?
lines: The old product took one description and built it.
But people find out what they want by seeing a first try.
So the description became a draft: come back to it, change it, build it again.
quote: Ideas rarely show up fully formulated.
close: We design for the second and third attempt, not only the first.
alt: The sixth bet: draft state matters

q: How do you give proof for something made a minute ago?
lines: A generated tool has no reviews, no maker, no history.
So its page carries what it does have.
How fast it was built, how often it has run, what it takes and gives, and the tools most like it.
quote: generated in x seconds, the equivalent of y dev hours
from: a note on the third round
close: We find what counts as evidence for a new kind of thing.
alt: A tool's page: built in 48 seconds, run 300 times

q: How do you decide what not to build?
lines: Search would have been easy to add. So would free runs, and a place for the merely curious.
Each was weighed against the one act that mattered: making a tool.
Each one lost.
quote: there is no point in replacing create with a far lower quality action
from: a note on the fourth round
close: We keep the product about one act, and say no to the rest out loud.
alt: The third round of wireframes

q: How do you design for the day something is missing?
lines: A tool made by a machine may have no description, no author, nothing like it.
A person may have no credits left.
So each page was drawn for that day too, not only the day everything is there.
quote: If no description, how do we fail gracefully?
from: a note beside the final screens
close: We draw the empty and broken states with the same care as the full ones.
alt: The last round, with its list of edge cases

q: How do you make a stranger feel a tool is for them?
lines: Before what it does, people ask whether they belong here.
So every example at the front was chosen for a feeling someone already has.
A chore they hate. A paid app they resent. A thing they have been meaning to sort out.
quote: Who are the right people for this product (do I belong here?)
close: We pick the examples for the people, not for the technology.
alt: Who the product is for

q: How do you find the product inside the product?
lines: Users were lost almost everywhere, and delighted in one place.
A small helper that read your description and made it better.
We built the new product around that conversation.
quote: The prompt helper is genius.
close: We look for the one moment people already love, and give it the room.
alt: The conversation on the left, the spec and the build on the right

q: How do you make the first visit worth a second?
lines: Nobody takes up a tool like this in one sitting.
So the first visit is not asked to do everything.
It has to leave you with one thing that worked, and a reason to bring your own problem next time.
quote: Let the user feel they have created / found / can show something of value for the time invested
close: We design the first ten minutes to earn the next visit, not to close the sale.
alt: The eighth bet: users want it done

q: How do you make a product you only have to learn once?
lines: Every tool, however odd, has the same three parts.
What goes in, what comes out, the steps between.
The first box asks for them, the spec lists them, the run shows them.
quote: Describe the inputs, outputs and steps.
from: a note on the last round
close: We find the one structure a product can repeat everywhere, so it only has to be learned once.
alt: The second round, with the first spec pages

q: How do you promise speed without promising everything?
lines: Taken at its word, the product promised the moon.
People believed it, tried something it could not do, and left.
So the promise got narrower and truer: these kinds of things, faster.
quote: I’m taking it at face value so my expectations are super high.
close: We set the promise where the product can keep it.
alt: The headline and the line under it

q: How do you tell someone no before it costs them?
lines: The machine cannot build everything, and used to say so only after trying.
By then the person had spent credits and patience.
So the answer moved forward, into the conversation, before anything is built.
quote: It has told me before I’ve spent any credits attempting to build it which is nice
from: the team, walking the old flow
close: We move the bad news to the cheapest moment.
alt: The two flows: exploring and creating

q: How do you get a team to see its product as a stranger does?
lines: The people who built it could no longer not know how it works.
So we walked the old flow with them, and each wrote what a newcomer is thinking at every step.
The gaps went up on the wall in their own words.
quote: I’m not sure if there is anything I need during the build phase. Do I just sit and wait?
from: the team, walking the old flow
close: We get the team to find the problem themselves, so the fix is theirs too.
alt: The old flow, with what the user is thinking at each step
